name: Ursolic acid
short: Given intravenously as liposomes to healthy volunteers and tumour patients, it caused dose-limiting liver toxicity and diarrhoea; one oral trial's abstract gives no adverse event data.
text: In a phase I trial of single intravenous infusions of ursolic acid liposomes (an injected drug formulation, not an oral supplement) in 59 healthy adult volunteers and 4 patients with advanced solid tumours, dose-limiting toxicity occurred at the three highest doses and consisted of hepatotoxicity and diarrhoea; other adverse events included nausea, abdominal distension, microscopic blood in the urine, raised serum sodium and skin rash. A multiple-dose phase I trial of the same intravenous liposomes, given on 14 consecutive days of each 21-day cycle to people with advanced solid tumours (21 in three dose cohorts plus 8 more for pharmacokinetics), observed no grade 3 or higher adverse events. A systematic review of its pharmacology describes ursolic acid as having some undesirable adverse effects and even toxicological activities; the abstract does not say what these are. For ursolic acid taken by mouth, a 12-week placebo-controlled trial in 24 adults with metabolic syndrome does not report adverse events in its abstract. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
